# The prompt list

Everything in this repository — the pooled cohort, the matched analysis, the
figures, the manuscript — was produced by asking an agent in ordinary
sentences. This file is that list of sentences, verbatim, in order.

Nothing here is a magic incantation. They are the questions a colleague would
ask, which is the point of the exercise; the work is in reading what comes back.

> ⚠️ **You will not get identical numbers.** An agent writes its own scripts,
> and two runs make different reasonable choices (which covariates, which
> caliper, ascending or descending). The published result is stable to about
> ±0.05 on the hazard ratio; see [`live-demo/reference-run/`](../live-demo/reference-run/)
> for what one full run produced and [`PIPELINE.md`](PIPELINE.md) for the
> ranges the acceptance checks allow.

## Three ways to run it

| Route | What you type | Time | Pace |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A · guided** | one sentence, then `next` 32 times | 60–100 min | You stop between every step. Acceptance checks after each. |
| **B · walkthrough** | the 14 prompts below | ~35 min | The shape of the work, start to finish, no methodology arguments. |
| **C · long** | the 18 prompts below | ~65 min | The same study with the arguments kept in. |

Route A is the one to use if you want to *learn* it; B and C are what the
recordings show. All three end in a manuscript whose every number came out of
a file on disk.

---

## Route A — guided, one mission at a time

Open this repository in Claude Code (or any agent that can read files and run
Python) and say:

```text
follow the ./live-demo mission by mission
```

That is the entire input. The agent reads [`live-demo/README.md`](../live-demo/README.md),
executes Mission 0.1, runs its acceptance script, summarises what it found, and
stops. You then drive it with four words:

| You say | It does |
|---|---|
| `next` | the next mission |
| `skip` | skips, and tells you what downstream missions that breaks |
| `why` | explains the *methodological reason* for the step, without advancing |
| `?` | re-explains *what just happened*, in plain language, without advancing |

Nine chapters, 32 missions, from ten raw hospital CSVs to a typeset preprint.
Each mission declares its output filenames, and
[`live-demo/verify/`](../live-demo/verify/) checks them against hard numbers —
so a run that quietly went wrong fails loudly instead of producing a
confident-looking manuscript.

```bash
cd live-demo && ../.venv/bin/python verify/run_all.py   # check a finished run
```

Before running it in front of anyone:

```bash
cd live-demo && ../.venv/bin/python verify/preflight.py --full
```

## Routes B and C — the recorded sessions

Both recordings ran in a scratch directory containing **only the raw inputs**:
the ten hospital CSVs and the site catalogue. No scripts, no notes, no
reference solutions. The agent wrote every line of analysis code during the
session.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/run && cd /tmp/run
cp -R /path/to/IMBrave150-mock/hospitals .
cp /path/to/IMBrave150-mock/hospitals_meta.csv .
```

and a `CLAUDE.md` in that directory holding the working rules — narrow output
so it projects, no libraries the environment does not have:

```markdown
# Working rules

- Python is `/path/to/IMBrave150-mock/.venv/bin/python`. It has pandas, numpy, lifelines and
  matplotlib. No sklearn, no statsmodels — write logistic regression yourself
  with numpy if you need it.
- Work in this directory. Write scripts as files, then run them.
- This session is projected on a 105-column screen. Keep output narrow and
  short: the numbers that matter, never a whole dataframe.
- Lead with the number, then the caveat. Answer in English.
```

Then start the agent and paste the prompts below one at a time, waiting for
each to finish. To reproduce the recording itself, including the slide breaks
and the chapter markers, run the recorder instead:

```bash
slides/tools/record_walkthrough.sh    # route B  → slides/cast/walk.cast
slides/tools/record_talk.sh           # route C  → slides/cast/talk-full.cast
```

It needs `tmux`, `asciinema`, `presenterm` and `bat`, and it drives a real
nested agent session — expect it to take as long as the recording.

## Route B — the walkthrough

The ordinary shape of a study: data, cleaning, exploring, analysis, writing. Recorded as [`slides/cast/walk.cast`](../slides/cast/walk.cast) (33 min) and playable at <https://imbrave150-talk.pages.dev/talk>.

**14 prompts.** Source: [`slides/tools/record_walkthrough.sh`](../slides/tools/record_walkthrough.sh)

### Slide break — The ordinary shape of a study

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/00-open.md` — 3 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

### Slide break — The data

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/01-data.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

**At the shell** (what arrived):

```bash
ls hospitals/
bat --style=header --line-range 1:2 hospitals/H01_Northshore_University.csv
bat --style=header --line-range 1:2 hospitals/H03_Metropolitan_Cancer_Ctr.csv
```

**Prompt 1** · *what is this data*

```text
There are ten CSV files in hospitals/ and a hospitals_meta.csv. Tell me what this data is: how many patients in total, how many per file, what the columns mean, and what the outcome variables are. Do not change anything yet.
```

### Slide break — Cleaning

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/02-clean.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

**Prompt 2** · *one table*

```text
The ten files do not use the same column names or the same units. Merge them into one table and write it to pooled.csv. Tell me every conversion you had to make, and attach each hospital's type and region from hospitals_meta.csv.
```

**Prompt 3** · *what is missing*

```text
Which columns have missing values, and how much? Is any of it structural rather than random? Tell me how you would handle each one and why, before you do anything about it.
```

### Slide break — Exploring

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/03-explore.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

**Prompt 4** · *who are these patients*

```text
Describe this cohort the way a Table 1 would: age, sex, aetiology, performance status, stage, liver function, and the two treatment groups. Keep it to one table I can read on screen.
```

**Prompt 5** · *how do the sites differ*

```text
Now compare the ten hospitals with each other. For each one: how many patients, what proportion got each drug, and what proportion have died. Sort it so the pattern is visible, and tell me what you see.
```

**Prompt 6** · *are the arms comparable*

```text
Compare the two treatment groups at baseline, covariate by covariate, and tell me which ones are meaningfully different and in which direction. Then tell me what that would do to a naive comparison of survival.
```

**Prompt 7** · *what does follow-up look like*

```text
How long were these patients followed, and how many events are there in each arm? Show me the distribution of follow-up time, and say whether it differs between the groups.
```

**Prompt 8** · *a picture*

```text
Make one figure that shows me what you think is the most important thing you have found so far, and save it. Tell me why you chose that one.
```

### Slide break — Analysis

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/04-analyse.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

**Prompt 9** · *the naive comparison*

```text
Compare overall survival between the two arms with no adjustment at all. Give me the Kaplan-Meier curves, the median survival in each group, and the hazard ratio, and save the figure.
```

**Prompt 10** · *account for the differences*

```text
Now account for the baseline differences you found earlier, using whatever method you think fits, and tell me why you chose it before you run it. Report the adjusted hazard ratio and how many patients the method could actually use.
```

**Prompt 11** · *does it hold up*

```text
Does the result hold in the subgroups a reviewer would ask about? Decide the list first, tell me it, then run them and show me a forest plot.
```

### Slide break — Writing it up

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/05-write.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

**Prompt 12** · *methods*

```text
Write the Methods section into manuscript.md, reconstructed from the scripts you actually ran rather than from memory. Include the software versions.
```

**Prompt 13** · *results*

```text
Now append the Results. Every number must come from a file on disk, and mark which file each one came from.
```

**Prompt 14** · *read it back*

```text
Read manuscript.md back and check it against the files. Is there any number in it you cannot trace to a source, or any claim the data do not support?
```

### Slide break — What this was

`presenterm --present slides/walkthrough/06-close.md` — 1 page(s). Nothing is asked of the agent here; this is where the presenter talks.

The same study with the methodology kept in: an ambiguous prompt that moves the answer, 120 analytic paths, four independent reviewers. Recorded as [`slides/cast/talk-full.cast`](../slides/cast/talk-full.cast) (64 min) and playable at <https://imbrave150-talk.pages.dev/talk-long>.

## Reading the answers back

The prompts are the easy half. What makes the result trustworthy is what you
do with each reply, and it is the same four habits every time:

1. **Ask for the plan before the run.** Several prompts above say *"tell me
   why you chose it before you run it"*. A method you agreed to in advance is
   one you can defend; a method you found in the output is one you are stuck
   with.
2. **Make it name its sources.** *"Every number must come from a file on disk,
   and mark which file each one came from."* This is what makes the audit in
   the next step possible at all.
3. **Ask it to check its own work against the files.** Each route closes on
   this, and in the recorded runs it found real defects — an unsourced number,
   a claim the data did not support, a script that was not idempotent.
4. **Run the acceptance checks anyway.** `live-demo/verify/` does not care what
   the agent said it did.

See [`PIPELINE.md`](PIPELINE.md) for what each step consumes and produces, and
[`FILE-TREE.md`](FILE-TREE.md) for where everything lands.
